sections.body: When the interrogative pronoun 哪 is used in a question, the structure is 哪 plus a measure word or noun plus another noun. sections.title: The Interrogative Particle 呢
sections.body: The interrogative particle 呢 is used after a noun or pronoun to form a question about a situation mentioned previously. The common sentence pattern is A……。B呢？ which means A…. What about B? This particle allows you to ask a parallel question about another person or thing in relation to what was just stated.

sections.title: Numbers Below 100
sections.body: Chinese numbers from 1 to 99 follow a consistent pattern. The basic digits are: 1 yī, 2 èr, 3 sān, 4 sì, 5 wǔ, 6 liù, 7 qī, 8 bā, 9 jiǔ. Tens are formed by combining the digit with shí (10): 10 shí, 20 èrshí (two tens), 30 sānshí (three tens), and so on up to 90 jiǔshí (nine tens). Numbers between tens are formed by stating the tens place followed by the ones digit. For example, 19 is shíjiǔ (ten nine), 23 is èrshísān (two tens three), 56 is wǔshíliù (five tens six), 88 is bāshíbā (eight tens eight), and 99 is jiǔshíjiǔ (nine tens nine).

sections.title: The 有 Sentence: Indicating Existence
sections.body: The verb 有 can be used in an existential sentence to indicate that a person or thing exists in a particular location or place. The basic structure is: Location + 有 + Person/Thing.

rows: Under the chair there is a small dog
In the school there is a shop
On the table there is a computer and a book

sections.title: Expression of Time with 点 and 分
sections.body: In Chinese, time is expressed using 点 (o'clock) for hours and 分 (minutes) for minutes, following the principle of larger units before smaller units. When expressing a whole hour, use 点 alone. When expressing minutes past the hour, use the pattern 点 + 分. Note that for 2 o'clock, always use 两点 (liǎng diǎn) rather than 二点 (èr diǎn). When minutes are less than ten, you can include 零 (líng, meaning zero) before the single digit minute.

sections.title: Distinguishing Morning and Afternoon
sections.body: To specify whether a time is in the morning or afternoon, add 上午 (morning) or 下午 (afternoon) before the time expression. The pattern is 上午/下午 + 点 + 分.

When expressing a whole hour, use 点 alone. When expressing minutes past the hour, use the pattern 点 + 分. Note that for 2 o'clock, always use 两点 (liǎng diǎn) rather than 二点 (èr diǎn). When minutes are less than ten, you can include 零 (líng, meaning zero) before the single digit minute.

sections.title: Distinguishing Morning and Afternoon
sections.body: To specify whether a time is in the morning or afternoon, add 上午 (morning) or 下午 (afternoon) before the time expression. The pattern is 上午/下午 + 点 + 分.

sections.body: An action in progress can be expressed by adding the adverb 在 before a verb or by using the modal particle 呢 at the end of a sentence. You can use 在 alone, 呢 alone, or both together.

sections.title: Negative Form of Actions in Progress
sections.body: The negative form is 没在 or 没 plus a verb or verb phrase. Note that 呢 cannot be used at the end of negative sentences expressing actions in progress.

sections.title: 了 Indicating Occurrence or Completion at the End of a Sentence
sections.body: 了 can be used at the end of a sentence to indicate that an action has occurred or been completed.

rows: He went to learn to drive.

sections.title: 了 Between a Verb and Its Object
sections.body: 了 can also be used between a verb and its object. There is usually a modifier before the object of the verb, such as a numeral classifier, an adjective, or a pronoun.

rows: She bought a little bit of apples.
I bought quite a few clothes.
How many people did you see?

sections.title: Negative Form of 了
sections.body: The negative form of 了 in both cases above is 没 plus the verb and object. In the negative form, 了 should be omitted.

rows: She did not go to the store.
I did not see Mr. Zhang.

sections.title: The Adverb 都
sections.body: 都 means both or all. It expresses totality or inclusion of everything in a group. The key rule is that the people or objects being included must come before 都 in the sentence.

rows: They all like to drink tea.
All of these are Wang Fang's things.
